articles.title: How India became dangerously addicted to Chinese imports
articles.summary: India’s toy shops provide an unlikely barometer by which to measure its economic relationship with China.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Xi and Modi have vowed to address growing trade imbalances By Nikhil Inamdar Mumbai 
- Published 5 October 2026 
Take a walk into an Indian toy shop and as well as picking up a new favourite plaything for a child, you might just get an insight into how the nation is battling for a better economic relationship with its all-powerful neighbour China. 
Six years ago, in an attempt to push local manufacturing and keep substandard toys out of its market, India raised tariffs on imported toys from 20% to 60% and eventually to 70%. 
Retailers were up in arms and said that domestic firms could never match the foreign-made stuff. But the combination of higher customs duties and quality control standards worked. 
Indian imports of toys fell by a third from nearly $300m (£227m) in 2020 to $100m this year, while exports rose from around $129m to $200m in the same period. Moreover, the country was able to drastically reduce its dependence on China, which held a 70% share of the local toy market. 
The sector stands out as a rare exception in India's otherwise unsuccessful attempts to rebalance an increasingly lopsided trading relationship with its larger neighbour, which some experts say, is now among the most asymmetric in the world. 
Even as diplomatic ties between the two countries completely broke down following the Galwan Valley clashes in 2020 and Delhi announced a slew of anti-dumping duties and a ban on Chinese apps such as Tik Tok, its trade deficit with Beijing has only ballooned - from $44bn in 2020 to an eye-popping $112bn this year. 
"India's economic dependence on China continued to deepen while political, security, and investment ties were at their lowest point," Kevin Zongzhe Li, a Washington-based Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Centre for China Analysis, told the BBC. 
More worryingly, exports to China remained below pre-pandemic level even as imports doubled in this period. 
"China now supplies over 30% of India's industrial imports, and India depends on it for more than 100 critical products. And the imbalance is worsening," says Ajay Srivastava of the Delhi-based Global Trade and Research Initiative (GTRI). 
If the rapid pace of imports continues, bilateral deficit could jump to $134bn, giving Beijing even more leverage over Indian industry, according to Srivastava. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Anti-China sentiment hit a fever pitch post border skirmishes in 2020, but relations have now thawed 
On the sidelines of the Brics summit in Delhi in September, amid a deepening thaw between the Asian giants, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping vowed to address , external these "structural trade imbalances and supply chain issues". 
But given how deeply entrenched Chinese imports have become to India's industrial economy, this will be a formidable task for Delhi, experts told the BBC. 
That's primarily because India depends on China to not merely consume end-products, but increasingly to produce industrial goods. 
To be true, India has reduced its reliance on imports of finished goods such as smartphones and solar equipment, and now produces more than a quarter of the world's iPhones. 
"Yet, production remains largely assembly-based and depends heavily on imported components, particularly from China," says Srivastava. 
It's the same story with industrial machinery, battery inputs, chemicals, solar cells, and manufacturing equipment. 
Electrical machinery and electronics alone account for 36% of imports, followed by machinery and mechanical appliances at 21.7%, while organic chemicals and plastics also have a significant share, according to the Observer Research Foundation (ORF) think tank. 
"Their interruption would not merely affect consumption; it would disrupt production itself," according to Soumya Bhowmik, a Fellow at ORF's Centre for New Economic Diplomacy, who argues that this reflects India's difficulty in substituting Chinese inputs with local production. 
Besides a growing reliance on inputs and raw material, Chinese imports to India are also being propelled by other macroeconomic trends. 
China has huge excess capacity in sectors from steel to solar panels and electric vehicles, while its slowing economy cannot absorb the output. 
Manufacturers are therefore increasingly turning to overseas markets, selling goods cheaply. China's trade surplus is expected to top $1tn for a second straight year. 
A lot of these goods are coming to Indian shores because it is rapidly expanding manufacturing across segments of the economy, but also as "Western markets impose tariffs and other restrictions", says Srivastava. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
India has reduced smartphone imports but depends heavily on China for components 
On the other hand, lack of access to the Chinese market remains a major challenge for Indian companies. 
"Indian products face a variety of tariff and non-tariff hurdles in China that make it difficult to scale exports," says Li. 
"If normalisation [of ties] continues without a serious push for reciprocal market access, India risks a situation where the political relationship improves but the economic dependency stays the same." 
The long term solution to both reducing avoidable imports and improving exports performance will be to strengthen manufacturing, says Srivastava. 
But that requires sector-specific industrial policy and stronger fundamentals – affordable power and credit, efficient logistics and stable regulations – areas where India still falls short. 
India has also recently softened foreign direct investment rules, which could open the door to Chinese companies wanting to expand Indian investments. But these too will need careful vetting, he adds. 
"Investment that merely expands distribution networks or assembles products using Chinese parts could increase imports and deepen dependence. Approvals should therefore prioritise technology transfer, local value addition, domestic component production and exports from India." 
More immediately, India could focus on targeting higher exports to China in specific sectors to reduce its trade asymmetry, says Li. Sectors like pharmaceuticals could be a natural fit with China's population aging and healthcare costs rising. 
"But narrowing a $112bn deficit won't come from finding niche export sectors alone," he adds. 
"The key question is whether Beijing is ready and willing to make concessions on market access as part of the broader normalisation. Alternatively, India will need to find its own leverage to force that conversation."

articles.title: UK university asks staff to review some partnerships with China after MI5 warning
articles.summary: The UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Staff at QUB have been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI" By Robbie Meredith 
Education and arts correspondent, BBC News NI 
- Published 4 October 2026 
Queen's University of Belfast (QUB) has asked staff to review some partnerships with China after a warning from MI5. 
In a highly unusual move, the UK's internal security service had warned universities they may have unintentionally assisted China's espionage. 
MI5 said the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) was a front company working for China's intelligence and security service. 
However, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in London said the accusation was "imaginary and purely fabricated". 
Staff at Queen's have now been "strongly advised to review any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI". 
"Work is ongoing within Queen's to do this," an email to staff said. 
"However, this may not be obvious through our existing systems and so researchers are also advised to undertake appropriate due diligence to identify the ultimate source of funding for collaborations with Chinese institutions." 
MI5 issued the alert for UK universities about CGTRI which it said had "very strong ties" to the Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS). 
Universities in the UK often collaborate and partner with universities elsewhere in the world to share research and expertise. 
But MI5 said it had identified more than 100 UK-linked academics who had contributed to projects funded by Ministry of State Security via CGTRI. 
It said that in some cases the researchers would not be aware of the front company's role in their project. 
UK academics have contributed to CGTRI-funded projects on topics including AI, cyber-security, covert communications systems and steganography, which means hiding a secret message or file inside an ordinary message or object. 
MI5 added that academics who failed to cut ties with CGTRI could ultimately face criminal charges for aiding a foreign state. 
As a result, UK universities were advised to immediately review the funding of any research collaboration with China. 
A QUB spokesperson told BBC News NI that the university takes "responsibilities around research and national security extremely seriously". 
"Queen's University has commenced a review around any existing or proposed collaborations involving CGTRI," they said. 
"We have also contacted staff requesting they review any existing or proposed collaborations with them and report any concerns to the relevant Faculty Dean of Research. 
"We will keep this situation under review while continuing to support our collaboration, research and innovation projects locally, nationally and internationally." 
According to its website, QUB has invested over $10m (£7.56m) in China-related research in areas like sustainable energy, information technology, food security and cancer research over the past decade. 
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Ulster University said they had no research links with the organisation referenced by MI5.

articles.title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
articles.summary: The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations.
articles.full_text:
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Rajapaksa was arrested two days after returning to Sri Lanka from Singapore By BBC Sinhala   and   Yvette Tan 
- Published 7 October 2026 
Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital. 
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday. 
They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital. 
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government. 
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated. 
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October. 
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred. 
Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president. 
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine. 
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled. 
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family. 
Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand. 
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

articles.title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
articles.summary: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead By Azadeh Moshiri South Asia correspondent 
- Published 6 October 2026 
At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month. 
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites. 
With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead. 
Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati. 
The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave. 
"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says. 
He has little doubt they are dead. 
But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave 
Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month. 
Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance. 
Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death. 
But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare. 
"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari. 
He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues. 
For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate. 
When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods 
Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them. 
Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed. 
Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data. 
The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol. 
The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over. 
Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality. 
Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue. 
"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC. 
He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to. 
For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses. 
Image source, Supplied Image caption, 
More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief 
The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households. 
This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family. 
The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster. 
Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied. 
"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities." 
The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution. 
In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required. 
The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn). 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing 
At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy. 
Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects. 
Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming. 
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders. 
This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster. 
For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar. 
He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati. 
But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village. 
Once again, he is without a home. 
"I have lost everything," he said. 
So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal. 
Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies. 
He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home. 
Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari

articles.title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
articles.summary: Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague has prompted calls for more transparency from Russia.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk By Vicky Wong   and   Gabriela Pomeroy 
- Published 7 October 2026 
US President Donald Trump says he has a call set up with Vladimir Putin about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia. 
Russian officials say they are investigating the death of the 28-year-old employee and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic. 
Trump told reporters on Wednesday evening he did not believe it was a bioweapon, adding "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." 
"If you listen to them, it's under control," he said, referring to Russian authorities. 
"We hope it is," he added. Reports emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation after the death. 
Referring to China's initial response to the Covid pandemic, Trump said: "Well, China didn't say much, and Russia is not saying much either. But they do say they have it very much under control." 
Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. 
Trump said the US was in "deep discussions" with Russia, but the Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled. 
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for more transparency from Russia, and requested further information on the lab tests on the individual who died. 
"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, adding that the WHO was also seeking "verification of media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause." 
Ghebreyesus called on Russia to provide "timely, complete and transparent information" in order to clarify "conflicting reports" and help the WHO assess the potential public health risks. 
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information". 
The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request. 
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier. 
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents. 
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region". 
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected". 
Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks". 
This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low." 
Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country. 
Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency. 
There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said. 
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities". 
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection. 
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia. 
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed. 
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early. 
People can be infected through: 
- 
infected flea bites 
- 
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials 
- 
the inhalation of respiratory particles 
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm. 
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area. 
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death . 
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title: Chinese runner dropped by sponsor after riding bike during marathon
articles.summary: Sun Yuanyuan was seemingly pictured on the back of another person's bike during part of the Berlin Marathon.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
The influencer was seen riding a bike during the Berlin Marathon, which took place at the end of September By Emer Moreau 
- Published 5 hours ago 
A Chinese fitness influencer has been dropped by her sponsor after she apologised for riding a bicycle during the Berlin marathon. 
Sun Yuanyuan, known as Abeeeer on Chinese social media, had claimed a personal best during the event which was held in September. 
But an Instagram page dedicated to monitoring inaccurate or misleading race times posted by influencers published a picture which appeared to show Sun on a bicycle between the 35km and and 40km marks. 
Sun apologised and admitted to "breaking the rules". Brooks, the running shoe company, has ended its sponsorship deal with her and her finish time has been disqualified by the marathon organisers. 
An Instagram account calling itself the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) posted a photo of Sun apparently on the back of a bike being ridden by another person during the marathon. 
The page also posted a grid of Sun's "splits" - which are the times taken to complete different 5km segments of the race. 
The grid appears to show that she sped up between the 35 and 40km marks, when she was allegedly on the bike. 
Sun posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, admitting that she had broken the rules. 
She wrote: "I won't make any excuses for this behaviour. 
"I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules. 
"My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon." 
Sun, who has 520,000 followers on Rednote, also said she "deliberately concealed" her actions, adding: "I feel deeply guilty about this." 
Brooks confirmed to BBC News that it had dropped Sun. 
A company statement said: "Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition. 
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual and publicly addressed the matter." 
OMTIU was set up to highlight "the growing trend of GPS-based fabrication, selective Strava displays and false PR claims" among marathon runners, particularly fitness influencers. Strava is a fitness tracking app. 
The page's mission statement says: "We exist to protect the integrity of the sport by ensuring that the times athletes share publicly reflect the times they actually ran." 
Its Instagram bio describes it as "satire". 
BBC News has contacted the Berlin Marathon for comment.

articles.title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
articles.summary: The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Pneumonic plague is often described as the most virulent form of plague By Dominic Hughes 
Health correspondent 
- Published 6 October 2026 
The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory. 
It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation. 
Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague. 
So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it? 
What is pneumonic plague? 
Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague. 
There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood. 
Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types. 
Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood. 
It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague. 
The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases. 
Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States. 
Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford. 
He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis , persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world. 
"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa. 
"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact." 
How does it spread? 
Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas. 
You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal. 
But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact. 
You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs. 
Some theories suggest that pneumonic plague was one of the main drivers behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century. 
Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague. 
"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said. 
"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form. 
"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism. 
"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks." 
Can it be treated? 
According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours. 
If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal. 
But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early. 
Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health. 
"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease. 
"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age. 
"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early. 
"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine." 
In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague. 
The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened. 
US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States". 
The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

articles.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
articles.summary: Some running in November's elections are deciding whether to distance themselves from an unpopular president who still dominates his party.
articles.full_text:
By Anthony Zurcher North America correspondent in Florida 
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will. 
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week. 
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy. 
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax". 
The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high. 
According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall. 
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular. 
"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue." 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Some polls suggest that many of Trump's policies, including the ongoing conflict with Iran, are unpopular 
That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump? 
Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free. 
The economy looming large 
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida. 
But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns. 
Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement. 
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight. 
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive." 
He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet". 
In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces. 
But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages. 
Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices. 
It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction. 
"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long." 
Image caption, 
"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll 
Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable". 
"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America." 
And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda". 
"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said. 
Image caption, 
Many candidates are campaigning hard on economic concerns 
Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran. 
For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies. 
The Donalds-Donald relationship 
Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website. 
It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself. 
"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!" 
Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor. 
"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor." 
While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism. 
Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, 
Trump's immigration crackdown is popular with most Republicans - but some told the BBC they feared friends and family could be targeted 
Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries. 
According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution. 
"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic." 
Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president. 
The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short. 
Image source, EPA Image caption, 
For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital 
It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole. 
"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job." 
He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy. 
The Republican messaging 
In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties. 
"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week. 
According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most. 
"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said. 
With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign. 
That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right. 
"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'" 
Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama. 
He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska. 
Image caption, 
"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa 
However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike. 
He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are. 
"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job." 
Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight. 
If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him. 
"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me." 
But if Republicans get punished at the ballot box in November, whether they run with the president or away from him, Trump will bear the brunt of the consequences - in the form of a hostile Congress with legislative and oversight powers - for the last two years of his presidency.
